word:lxx:L700016.explanation: Abar, also rendered Avar, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 8:17. Because it is a name, its meaning is primarily identifying rather than conceptual: it points to a particular named individual in the genealogical record. The word should therefore be read as a personal designation, with the surrounding verse supplying the person’s place in that record.

word:lxx:L700081.explanation: Abichail, also represented as Avikhel, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general description or action word, but a personal name used in genealogical and tribal records. The name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in Numbers and 1 Chronicles. Without the surrounding verse text, the specific individuals bearing this name cannot be distinguished here; the lexical meaning remains the name itself rather than a broader concept.

word:lxx:L700254.explanation: This Greek LXX adjective describes something that is unclear or unseen—something not plainly understood or not visible. It can point either to a lack of clarity or to something hidden from sight, depending on the sentence where it appears. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Psalms, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding wording.

word:lxx:L700302.explanation: Adōnaie, also given as “Athonee,” is a proper name in the Greek Septuagint. It identifies a named person or figure rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament text represented here, both times in Judges: Judges 13:8 and Judges 16:28. The name’s specific referent and significance in either passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L700377.explanation: This adjective describes someone as “gaining the prize.” It presents the person as attaining the reward or victory being sought, rather than merely striving toward it. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both in 3 Maccabees, but the surrounding verse text is not available here. Its exact force in either passage therefore depends on the sentence and context in which it appears.

word:lxx:L700485.explanation: Aischyno means to shame. It can also mean to be ashamed.

word:lxx:L700548.explanation: Akkarioth is a proper name, referring to a specific named place or entity rather than expressing a general action, quality, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it appears only once, at Jeremiah 31:41. The available lexical information preserves the name as “Akkariōth” or “Akkarioth,” but the surrounding verse text is not included here, so its precise role in that passage cannot be described further.

word:lxx:L700694.explanation: Alloioō means to make different or change. It can describe a changed appearance, as well as changes to times and seasons.

word:lxx:L700760.explanation: This proper name refers to an Amalekite, a person belonging to the people called Amalek. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for both one individual and the Amalekites as a group. The word occurs six times, in six verses, from 1 Samuel through 2 Samuel. Its references include 1 Samuel 15:6 and 2 Samuel 1:13, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain each specific use.

word:lxx:L700889.explanation: Amphitapos means a double-sided rug or tapestry.

word:lxx:L700957.explanation: Anaia, also rendered Anea, is a proper name identifying a named entity in the Greek Old Testament. It appears once in the LXX, at Nehemiah 10:23. The available information establishes the name’s form and location, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain whether it refers to a person, family, or place. Its meaning is therefore best represented as the proper name itself rather than expanded into an inferred description.

word:lxx:L700980.explanation: “Examine” means to investigate or inspect something in order to understand it or reach a judgment. As a verb, it describes an active process of looking into a matter, rather than simply seeing or noticing it. This Greek LXX word occurs four times: once in 1 Samuel and three times in Susanna. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea is the act of examination.

word:lxx:L701011.explanation: Ananeoō means to renew. It can describe renewing a friendship or league that people already had with one another.

word:lxx:L701068.explanation: “Relate” means to communicate something to another person. As a verb, it describes the act of making information, words, or an account known, rather than naming a person, place, or thing. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, this word appears eight times, from Leviticus through 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being related and the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L701086.explanation: Anaphoreus means a bearer. It can also mean a carrying pole.

word:lxx:L701165.explanation: Aniam is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:19. The available lexical information establishes the name’s identification, but does not provide an additional ordinary meaning or explanation of the person beyond the name itself. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding genealogical context.

word:lxx:L701253.explanation: This word is a proper name for a person called “Antiocheus” or “Antiokhefs.” It does not describe a general quality or action; it identifies an individual by name. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Maccabees 4, at 4:9 and 4:19. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain that person’s role in either passage.

word:lxx:L701374.explanation: This verb means to threaten: to express or communicate danger, harm, or punishment toward someone. It describes a forceful warning rather than a quiet statement, and its exact force depends on the surrounding sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs nine times, including passages from Genesis, Numbers, Isaiah, Nahum, Sirach, and 3 Maccabees. The word can describe a person’s threatening words or an announced threat. Its basic meaning remains the act of threatening.

word:lxx:L701459.explanation: This verb means to treasure something or store it away for safekeeping. It describes deliberately placing something valuable in reserve rather than using or discarding it immediately. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 3:4. The word’s central idea is preserving something precious so that it remains available and secure. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the act of treasuring or storing away.

word:lxx:L701576.explanation: This Greek Old Testament verb means “look at” or “keep watch.” It describes directing one’s attention toward something, whether by observing it or remaining alert for it. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, including two occurrences in Lamentations 4:17 and one in Habakkuk 2:1. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is attentive observation or watchful waiting.

word:lxx:L701598.explanation: Apostrephō means to turn away. It can also mean to alienate, describing a person’s revolt from someone else.

word:lxx:L701635.explanation: This noun means a “terse pointed saying; apophthegm”—a brief statement expressed in a memorable, striking way. It refers to a compact saying rather than a long speech or extended explanation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Deuteronomy and Ezekiel, so it is uncommon within this corpus. The surrounding verse determines what the particular saying communicates, but the word itself emphasizes the saying’s concise and pointed character.

word:lxx:L701693.explanation: This noun means “spider’s web,” the delicate network made by a spider. It refers to something associated with a spider or its web, rather than to the spider alone. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, in Job, Psalms, and Isaiah. Its ordinary meaning remains concrete and recognizable: a fragile web spun by a spider. The surrounding verse determines whether the word is being used simply as a physical image or as part of a comparison.

word:lxx:L701727.explanation: This noun means “valor”: courageous strength shown when facing difficulty, danger, or opposition. It describes a quality a person may possess and display through brave action, rather than an action word itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 25 times, especially in 4 Maccabees, where the word’s repeated use highlights the importance of courageous character. Its precise emphasis in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L701752.explanation: Aristoboulos is a personal name, also rendered “Aristovulos.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the name occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 1:10. The name’s precise significance for that individual cannot be determined from the name alone, and the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the person’s role in that passage.

word:lxx:L701950.explanation: Asiedōth, also rendered Asiethoth, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular place or location in the Greek Old Testament text. The name occurs once in the Greek form of the Old Testament, at Joshua 15:47. Without the surrounding verse text, its location within the list of places cannot be explained further, but its lexical function is clear: it serves as a geographic name.

word:lxx:L701987.explanation: Aspazomai means to greet or salute.

word:lxx:L702043.explanation: This noun means “asphalt,” a sticky, tar-like material. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, all in Genesis. The word identifies a physical substance rather than an action, quality, or person. Its exact role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains the material itself. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that corpus.

word:lxx:L702106.explanation: This noun means a “path with no turnings”: a route that proceeds directly rather than bending or winding. It identifies a straightforward way or track, with the central idea being the absence of turns. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times across Judges, Job, Wisdom, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains a direct, unturning path.

word:lxx:L702191.explanation: This noun means “menstruation,” referring to a woman’s monthly bodily bleeding. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used in passages that discuss the condition itself and the ritual-cleanliness regulations associated with it. The word occurs 11 times across 8 verses, mostly in Leviticus, with one occurrence in Ezekiel. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the menstrual period or the bleeding connected with it.

word:lxx:L702249.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something that is not opening the mouth. It presents a state of remaining closed at the mouth rather than speaking or opening it. The wording gives a precise physical description, while the surrounding verse would determine its particular force in context. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in Wisdom 19:17. Its meaning is therefore focused and specific: the mouth is not opened.

word:lxx:L702317.explanation: Achōi; Akhi is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:29. Because no verse text or surrounding passage is available here, the name itself can be stated confidently, while the person’s particular role must be understood from that passage’s context.

word:lxx:L702362.explanation: This word is a proper name, rendered “Badaia” and also associated with the form “Vathea.” It identifies a named individual or figure rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Ezra 10:35. The supplied lexical information gives the name’s form and rendering, but the verse text is not included here, so its specific role in that passage cannot be described further.

word:lxx:L702425.explanation: Baithmacha is a proper name, also given as Vethmakha. It does not describe an action, quality, or object in the ordinary sense; it identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs twice, both times in 2 Samuel, at 2 Samuel 20:14 and 20:15. Its precise reference is understood from the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a designation rather than as a general vocabulary term.

word:lxx:L702528.explanation: This adjective means “foreigner,” describing someone regarded as coming from another people or place. It identifies a person as an outsider in relation to the community or group being discussed, rather than naming a particular person or nation. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word occurs seven times. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a person viewed as foreign to those speaking or acting.

word:lxx:L702551.explanation: This adjective describes a person who is “heavy in spirit: indignant; sullen.” It refers to an inward disposition rather than an outward action, expressing a spirit weighed down by displeasure. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 6:20. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here, but its ordinary sense identifies an indignant or sullen state of spirit.

word:lxx:L702713.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “violate” or “force his way.” It describes pressing past a person’s will, resistance, or proper boundary rather than acting by willing agreement. As a verb, it expresses an action imposed through force. The word occurs 14 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, Judges, and 2 Samuel. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and situation.

word:lxx:L702858.explanation: Gabaōn is a proper name, rendered Gabaon.

word:lxx:L702924.explanation: This Greek LXX proper name refers to “Galaaditin” or “Galaathitin.” It functions as a name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The word appears seven times in the LXX corpus, across four Old Testament verses and three Deuterocanonical verses. Its precise referent is determined by the passage in which it appears, since the name itself does not provide a broader descriptive definition.

word:lxx:L702999.explanation: Gedsōn is a personal name, also rendered Yethson, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a particular person or persons in genealogical and tribal records. The name occurs 29 times across 28 verses, especially in Numbers and 1 Chronicles. Its meaning is therefore chiefly identifying: it marks a named individual within Israel’s recorded family and community history, while the surrounding passage determines which person bearing the name is intended.

word:lxx:L703075.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means a “dyke” or “dam”—a structure built to hold back, block, or control water. It refers to a physical barrier rather than an action or abstract idea. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings preserved in this corpus: once in Isaiah 37:25 and once in 2 Maccabees 12:13. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L703130.explanation: This adjective means “dark,” describing the absence or reduction of light. It can identify something characterized by darkness, whether referring to physical surroundings or another context where the surrounding passage supplies the precise force. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Job 10:21. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: it describes what is dark. The reference alone does not provide enough surrounding text to explain any further nuance in that verse.

word:lxx:L703192.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something capable of drawing. It points to the ability to make drawn figures or pictures, rather than naming the drawing itself. As an adjective, it normally modifies a person, skill, or object associated with that ability. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it appears once, at 3 Maccabees 4:20. The surrounding context determines exactly what or whom it describes in that passage.

word:lxx:L703219.explanation: This noun means “ball” or “small globe,” referring to a rounded object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Chronicles 4:12–13. The basic meaning points to a compact, spherical form rather than a person, action, or abstract idea. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding description, but the word itself identifies a rounded object.

word:lxx:L703336.explanation: This adjective describes something made up of ten months or lasting across a period of ten months. It gives a specific time span rather than expressing a general idea about length or duration. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 7:2. The word itself identifies the period as ten months; the surrounding verse is needed to understand exactly what person, event, or comparison it describes there.

word:lxx:L703466.explanation: This verb means “bend about” or “turn about,” describing an act of changing direction or curving around. It functions as an action word rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 4:34. The precise force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on bending or turning around.

word:lxx:L703488.explanation: Diakrinō means to discriminate or discern, distinguishing between good and evil.

word:lxx:L703664.explanation: Diexagō means to bring to an end.

word:lxx:L703761.explanation: This noun means “half”: one of two parts into which something is divided. It can refer to a portion produced by cutting or separating an object, rather than to the whole. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times across five verses, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, and Ezekiel. Its precise role in any particular verse depends on what has been divided and the surrounding sentence.

word:lxx:L703839.explanation: Dynamis means power or ability—the capacity to accomplish something.

word:lxx:L703884.explanation: This adjective describes something that has an unpleasant smell—something ill-smelling. It functions as a descriptive word, telling the reader about the odor of a person, object, or place rather than naming the thing itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 6:25. The available lexical meaning is clear, while the exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L703905.explanation: This verb means “bribe”: to give or use a bribe in order to influence someone improperly. It describes bribery as an action rather than naming the payment itself. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in Sirach and 3 Maccabees. The word’s central idea remains the use of gifts or payments to gain an unfair decision, favor, or advantage. The surrounding passage determines who is bribing and what outcome is being sought.

word:lxx:L704104.explanation: This noun means “dissimulation”: the act of hiding one’s true intention or feeling behind a false appearance. It describes deliberate pretense rather than open and sincere conduct. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 13:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is concealed purpose expressed through deceptive behavior.

word:lxx:L704287.explanation: This verb describes someone being awestruck—deeply affected by what they see, hear, or experience. It presents a person as overwhelmed with wonder or amazement rather than simply noticing something. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including passages in Ecclesiastes, Wisdom, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L704373.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “expire,” describing the ending of a person’s life. As a verb, it expresses what someone does or comes to do rather than naming a person, object, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, in Ezekiel 21:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the coming to an end of life.

word:lxx:L704409.explanation: Eleale, also rendered Eleali, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named place or locality rather than describing an action, quality, or person’s character. The name occurs five times in the LXX, in Numbers, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its normal function is simply to designate Eleale. It should therefore be read as a place-name, not translated as an ordinary descriptive word.

word:lxx:L704632.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “bear”: to carry, endure, or bring something, depending on the sentence. It is a verb, so it describes an action rather than a person or object. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 15:17. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly what is being borne there, but its basic meaning remains the act of bearing or carrying. word:lxx:L704647.explanation: “Enakim” is a proper name for a people or group named in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general description or an action word, but a specific designation used for the Enakim. This name occurs nine times in the LXX corpus, chiefly in Deuteronomy and Joshua, and also appears in Jeremiah. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L704690.explanation: This adjective describes someone “born in the house,” meaning the person was born within the household rather than being identified by a separate place of origin. It functions as a descriptive word for a person’s birth status. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 18:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains clear: a person born in the household.

word:lxx:L704715.explanation: This verb means to “usurp authority”: to take or exercise authority that does not properly belong to the person doing so. It describes an action rather than a person or title. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs twice, both in Sirach. The surrounding verse wording is needed to show exactly who is acting and how the misuse of authority functions in each passage, but the word’s central sense remains an improper taking or exercising of authority.

word:lxx:L704874.explanation: Exaptō means to attach or fasten something.

word:lxx:L704953.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “act of destruction”: a deed or process by which something is completely ruined or wiped out. It names the destructive action itself rather than describing a person or object. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at 1 Samuel 15:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the sentence where it appears.

word:lxx:L705028.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to set something up again or restore it. It describes the act of putting something back into a proper or previous condition, rather than merely beginning something new. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, both in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains renewal through reestablishing what had been damaged, displaced, or brought low.

word:lxx:L705051.explanation: This verb means “discharge at,” describing the act of sending or releasing something toward a person or place. It occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, all in four verses: three in Job and one in Ezekiel. The word’s precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains an active sending or releasing directed at a target.

word:lxx:L705183.explanation: Epikylindeō means to roll down upon.

word:lxx:L705370.explanation: This adverb means “seven-fold,” describing something done or present in an amount multiplied by seven. It expresses a seven-times measure rather than naming an object, person, or action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times: four times in Old Testament passages and once in Sirach. Its exact force—whether describing quantity, intensity, or repetition—depends on the sentence where it appears, but its central idea remains a sevenfold measure.

word:lxx:L705406.explanation: This adjective describes something as “bruised pounded.” It points to material that has been struck, crushed, or beaten so that its condition is marked by that treatment. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears once, in Leviticus 2:14. Its basic meaning is therefore specific rather than broad: it identifies something prepared or affected through pounding or bruising. The surrounding verse supplies the particular object and purpose, but the word itself focuses on the object's bruised or pounded condition.

word:lxx:L705543.explanation: Etē means a year or years.

word:lxx:L705617.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something as having a good reputation or being famous. It expresses honorable public recognition rather than merely being noticed. As an adjective, it adds this quality to a person, thing, or name being described. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice: once in Jeremiah and once in Wisdom. Its basic sense remains “of good report; famous,” while the surrounding sentence determines what is receiving that description.

word:lxx:L705662.explanation: This verb describes someone who is willing and ready to obey. It presents obedience as an inward readiness to respond favorably to direction or authority, rather than merely describing an outward act. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 8:6. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its basic sense is a person being inclined toward obedience.

word:lxx:L705749.explanation: This noun means a place for the training of youth—a location set apart for educating and preparing young people. It refers to a facility rather than to the young people themselves or to the act of training. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 4:9. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning identifies an institution devoted to youth instruction and development.

word:lxx:L705820.explanation: Zai is a noun functioning as a personal name or designation, not as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs only once, at Psalm 118:49. The available lexical information identifies the word itself, but without the verse text and surrounding context, it does not establish anything further about the person or role associated with Zai. Its precise significance in that verse must therefore be understood from the passage where it appears.

word:lxx:L705882.explanation: Ziza is a proper name, rendered “Ziza.” It identifies a person named in the Greek Old Testament rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 23:10–11 and 2 Chronicles 11:20. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not provide further meaning beyond identifying the individual or individuals called Ziza.

word:lxx:L705969.explanation: Eliam is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. It is rendered as “Ēliam” or “Iliam.” In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Ezekiel 47:16. The name itself identifies the person, but the available information does not provide the surrounding verse text or additional details about who Eliam was. Its precise significance in that passage therefore depends on reading the verse and its surrounding context.

word:lxx:L706120.explanation: This adjective describes someone as “bold” and “of good courage”—ready to act with confidence rather than fear. It is a character word, identifying a person or people as courageous. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 13:13. The word’s basic meaning is therefore a clear description of courage and inner confidence, while the surrounding verse determines exactly how that quality is expressed in context.

word:lxx:L706182.explanation: Themelioō means to lay a foundation or found something.

word:lxx:L706371.explanation: This word is a personal name, rendered “Iada” or “Iatha.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or spiritual concept. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles 9:42. Because the available information does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, the person’s identity and role cannot be stated more specifically here. The two approved forms, “Iada” and “Iatha,” represent the name’s recorded renderings in this LXX entry.

word:lxx:L706421.explanation: Ianouou is a personal name, appearing in the Greek Old Testament as the name of an individual. It is preserved in the forms “Ianouou” and “Ianuu,” rather than translated as a descriptive word. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 14:6. Without the verse text and its surrounding passage, the person’s role or significance cannot be stated from the name alone.

word:lxx:L706458.explanation: Iatreuō means to treat medically or cure.

word:lxx:L706599.explanation: Ierakōn, also rendered Ierakon, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:46. The name identifies a specific entity named in that passage, while the name itself does not carry a broader ordinary meaning such as an action, quality, or relationship. Its precise significance in Joshua depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L706612.explanation: Ieremin is a proper name, referring to a person identified by that name. It is not a general description or action word, but a personal designation used in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Jeremiah 42:3. The available lexical information gives the meaning simply as “Ieremin”; the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the person’s specific role or significance in that passage.

word:lxx:L706667.explanation: Iesrae, also rendered Iezrae, is a proper name rather than a descriptive word or action. It identifies a specific named individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 27:8. Since the available record gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its precise role in that passage cannot be described further here. The two forms, “Iesrae” and “Iezrae,” represent the same recorded name.

word:lxx:L706726.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “to cheer” or “make cheerful.” It describes bringing gladness or lifting someone’s spirits, rather than merely feeling cheerful oneself. As a verb, it expresses an action directed toward producing joy or encouragement. It occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, appearing once in Psalms and twice in Sirach. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is making someone or something cheerful.

word:lxx:L706825.explanation: This adjective describes something as “of equal value”—matching another thing in worth, strength, or significance. It presents two things as equivalent rather than ranking one above the other. In the Greek LXX material represented here, the word occurs twice, both in 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on what is being compared, but its central idea remains equality in value or capacity.

word:lxx:L706883.explanation: This word is a proper name, referring to a person called “Iōazae” or “Ioazae.” It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; its function is to identify an individual.
